Expedient

ek-SPEE-dee-uhnt -- from Latin expedire, 'to free the feet,' from ex- ('out') + pes/ped- ('foot') -- literally to disentangle the feet and get moving. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Expedient is convenient and advantageous.

Building a temporary footbridge was the most expedient way to reconnect the two halves of the flooded village.

Worked Example

A company facing a public complaint issues a quick refund instead of investigating what actually went wrong.

That quick, practical fix -- convenient for solving today's problem, even if it skips a deeper solution -- is exactly what expedient describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

convenient: suited to one's needs at the moment

pragmatic: dealing with things sensibly and realistically

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

impractical: not sensible or workable

idealistic: guided by principle rather than practical convenience

Where it sits · how much quick advantage drives the choice — convenient → expedient → pragmatic

convenient vs. expedient: Convenient is milder than expedient -- something convenient is simply easy or handy, while expedient specifically means chosen because it's the quickest practical fix for an immediate problem, sometimes overlooking a better long-term option.

pragmatic vs. expedient: Pragmatic is stronger than expedient in a different direction -- it describes a whole practical mindset or approach, while expedient usually describes one particular convenient choice made for the moment.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ex-

prefix — ex-: out (Latin)

root — -ped-

root — -ped-: foot (Latin (pes, pedis))

suffix — -ient

suffix — -ient: doing or being; forms an adjective (variant of -ent) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin expedire meant 'to free the feet' -- ex- ('out') plus ped- ('foot') -- and the suffix -ient forms the adjective. An expedient choice untangles your feet and gets things moving quickly, whether or not it is the noblest path.

Use the root in a new word: impede

Use the root in a new word: impede: A single broken elevator can impede deliveries to the building's upper floors for an entire afternoon.

Word Choice

Expedient often carries a faint hint of criticism -- an expedient choice solves the immediate problem but may sacrifice principle or thoroughness to do it quickly, which is different from something simply 'practical.'
